docs.title: Goose-Eyes
docs.text:
Autonomy code base for the 26-27 season. The runtime is a dora-rs dataflow: each node is its own process (Python today; Rust and C/C++ later), wired together by a YAML graph. The main platform is the Jetson Orin; see Setup for getting an environment on either it or a laptop.

This site is the hub: it documents how the system is structured and what each component's contract is (inputs, outputs, message types, rates). Generated API reference sits underneath in API Reference.

docs.title: System map
docs.text:
Everything that runs today lives in the dora dataflow. A ROS 2 / Nav2 navigation stack exists in a separate repo and will be brought in later; a dora ↔ ROS 2 bridge is planned but nothing in this repo depends on it yet.

flowchart LR
  subgraph dora["dora dataflow (goose-eyes/)"]
    direction LR
    camera["camera_capture"] -- image --> display["second_frame_displayer"]
    camera -- image --> rerun["rerun_image_test"]
  end
  subgraph ros["ROS 2 / Nav2 (planned, not in this repo)"]
    nav["Nav2"]
  end
  dora -. "planned bridge" .-> ros

docs.title: Where to look
docs.text: Setup pixi install, the jetson platform, adding a dev platform dora running the demos, architecture (generated graphs), per-node contracts API Reference Python module docs from docstrings; Rust / C++ slots reserved Updating the docs the three pixi run docs* tasks and the docs-update workflow

docs.title: Updating the docs
docs.text: The site is MkDocs + Material, configured in mkdocs.yml, with the pages in docs/. The toolchain is its own pixi environment (docs), so it never touches the runtime env; the tasks below find that environment on their own.

docs.title: The three commands
docs.text:
pixi run docs-serve    # live preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000 — edit a page, the browser reloads
pixi run docs          # full build into site/ with --strict: broken links and nav mistakes fail it
pixi run docs-gen      # only regenerate docs/generated/ (dora graph → Mermaid); the other two run it first

site/ is build output and gitignored. docs/generated/ is checked in — commit it when a dataflow changes, so a --strict build is reproducible without dora installed.

docs.title: When you change…
docs.text:
you changed update a dataflow YAML nothing by hand — pixi run docs-gen regenerates the diagram. If a node was added/removed, add/remove its page under docs/dora/nodes/ and its line in the nav: of mkdocs.yml. a node's inputs, outputs, metadata or rate its page in docs/dora/nodes/ — the tables are the contract; keep them true. a docstring nothing — the API pages are rendered from the source at build time. pixi.toml platforms or targets docs/setup/platforms.md / docs/setup/adding-a-platform.md. a page's location or name the nav: in mkdocs.yml, and any links to it (--strict will tell you).

Conventions: mark anything you don't know as TODO rather than guessing, and never write a "Why" for a decision you didn't make — a TODO: rationale is more useful than an invented one. Docstrings are Google style. Repo files that aren't pages get linked with a full GitHub URL, since MkDocs only resolves links inside docs/.

docs.title: The docs-update workflow (Claude Code skill)
docs.text:
For a batch of merged changes there's a Claude Code skill, docs-update, that does the judgment work this page describes: it diffs the repo since the last docs pass (docs/.last-docs-commit), works out which pages are affected, updates the contract tables, runs pixi run docs and fixes what --strict complains about, then prints a report (pages changed, new TODOs, functions missing docstrings, things it wasn't sure about). It does not commit and does not edit node source — you review the diff.

It lives at .claude/skills/docs-update/ on your machine and is deliberately not tracked (.claude/ is gitignored), so it's a personal tool, not part of the repo. Run it in Claude Code with /docs-update from the repo root, typically after merging to main. If you'd rather do the pass by hand, the table above is the whole checklist; just update docs/.last-docs-commit to HEAD afterwards so the next skill run starts from the right place.

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text:
Language Status Where it comes from Python live mkdocstrings reads the docstrings in goose-eyes/nodes/*.py statically at build time (Google style); one page per module, generated by utils/gen_api_pages.py, nothing checked in. Rust planned cargo doc output will be copied into site/api/rust/ by the docs task once there are Rust nodes. C/C++ planned Doxygen output will be copied into site/api/cpp/ the same way.

The Python pages only show what the docstrings say. Right now most node scripts have none — see Updating the docs for how the docs-update report lists them.

docs.title: dora
docs.text:
How the dora side is laid out and how to run the demos. The generated graph of every dataflow is on Architecture; each node's contract is under Nodes.

Everything lives in goose-eyes/: dataflows/ holds the dataflow graphs (*.yml) and nodes/ the scripts they run (a node's path: is resolved relative to the dataflow file, hence ../nodes/…). Logs for each run land in out/<run-id>/.

docs.title: Webcam fan-out demo
docs.text:
A simple dora-rs dataflow: one node captures webcam frames and fans them out to five display nodes over shared memory. It's a minimal example of how nodes, inputs and outputs are wired.

camera_capture.py ──image──┬──▶ displayer   (second_frame_displayer.py)
                           ├──▶ displayer2
                           ├──▶ displayer3
                           ├──▶ displayer4
                           └──▶ displayer5
File Role dataflows/dataflow.yml The graph: node ids, which script each runs, and how outputs feed inputs nodes/camera_capture.py Reads frames with OpenCV, flattens them to a pyarrow array and sends them on image (frame shape goes in metadata) nodes/second_frame_displayer.py Receives image, reshapes it back with the metadata, shows it in a window

Run it:

pixi run dora-demo

Press q in the camera capture node window to stop.

nodes/camera_capture.py opens camera index 2 (cv2.VideoCapture(2)). If you get camera didn't open, change the index to match your machine (0 is usually the built-in webcam).

docs.title: Rerun + dora
docs.text:
On the Jetson, pixi run install-rerun once first (see Platforms).

Run:

pixi run rerun-test       # dataflows/rerun-test.yml: camera → display + nodes/rerun_image_test.py (spawns the viewer)

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
One diagram per dataflow in goose-eyes/dataflows/, generated by dora graph <yml> --mermaid into docs/generated/ (pixi run docs-gen; the docs and docs-serve tasks run it first). Don't edit the diagrams by hand — change the YAML and regenerate. Node ids in the diagram are the id: fields in the YAML; the script each id runs is listed in the tables below.

Every edge carries the same payload today: a flattened BGR frame as a pyarrow uint8 array with shape and time in the metadata (see camera_capture).

docs.title: dataflow.yml — webcam fan-out demo
docs.text:
pixi run dora-demo. One capture node, five display nodes reading the same output over shared memory.

  displayer[/"**displayer**"\]
  displayer2[/"**displayer2**"\]
  displayer3[/"**displayer3**"\]
  displayer4[/"**displayer4**"\]
  displayer5[/"**displayer5**"\]
  camera -- image --> displayer
  camera -- image --> displayer2
  camera -- image --> displayer3
  camera -- image --> displayer4
  camera -- image --> displayer5
id script camera nodes/camera_capture.py displayer … displayer5 nodes/second_frame_displayer.py (five instances)

docs.title: rerun-test.yml — webcam into rerun
docs.text:
pixi run rerun-test. Same capture node; one OpenCV display and one node that logs the frames to a rerun viewer it spawns.

flowchart TB
  camera[\"**camera**"/]
  displayer[/"**displayer**"\]
  rerun[/"**rerun**"\]
  camera -- image --> displayer
  camera -- image --> rerun
id script camera nodes/camera_capture.py displayer nodes/second_frame_displayer.py rerun nodes/rerun_image_test.py

nodes/rerun_test.py is not in any dataflow — it's a standalone rerun sanity check (details).

docs.title: camera_capture
docs.text: goose-eyes/nodes/camera_capture.py — the source node: reads a webcam with OpenCV, resizes to 640×480, publishes each frame. ++q++ in its preview window stops it. Used as camera in both dataflows.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
output type metadata rate image pa.array(uint8), flattened BGR frame (480*640*3) shape: (480, 640, 3), time: float camera-limited (typically 30 fps). TODO: measure on the Jetson

Camera index is hard-coded (cv2.VideoCapture(2)); change it if you get error: camera didn't open.

docs.title: rerun_image_test
docs.text: goose-eyes/nodes/rerun_image_test.py — logs the camera stream to a rerun viewer it spawns. Used as rerun in rerun-test.yml.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text: input type metadata used rate image pa.array(uint8), flattened BGR frame shape, time follows camera_capture

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text: None on the dataflow; logs rerun entity camera/image. STREAM_ONLY = True keeps only the latest frame in the viewer (no timeline); set it to False for timestamped history.

docs.title: rerun_test
docs.text:
goose-eyes/nodes/rerun_test.py — not a dora node: rerun's "DNA abacus" example, connecting to an already-running viewer. A smoke test that the rerun install works.

pixi run rerun &
pixi run python goose-eyes/nodes/rerun_test.py

No inputs or outputs. TODO: keep as a pixi task, or delete.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
One pixi manifest covers the whole environment — Python and non-Python alike — for every platform, with a single pixi.lock solved for all of them at once.

curl -fsSL https://pixi.sh/install.sh | sh     # once
pixi install                                   # from the repo root
pixi run install-rerun                         # Jetson only — rerun lives outside the lock there

Then pixi run <task> / pixi run <cmd>, or pixi shell. pixi task list shows the tasks.

  • Adding a dependency: pixi add <pkg> (pixi add --pypi <pkg> for PyPI). It either resolves for every platform or fails right there, before anyone installs anything.
  • Jetson-only dependencies go under [target.jetson.*], laptop substitutes under [target.osx-arm64.*] — see Platforms for the reasoning and the JetPack-native OpenCV / TensorRT wiring.
  • Setting up another laptop OS? Adding a platform.
  • The docs toolchain is a separate pixi environment (docs); see Updating the docs.

docs.title: Adding a development platform
docs.text: The Jetson is the main target and osx-arm64 is the only dev platform declared so far. Adding another (say linux-64 for an x86 laptop) is mostly a pixi.toml exercise; these are the things that bite.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Declare it. Add the platform string to platforms = [...] in pixi.toml. Plain strings ("linux-64", "win-64", "osx-64") are fine for laptops; the Jetson entry is a named platform ({ name = "jetson", platform = "linux-aarch64", glibc = "2.39" }) only because it has to pin the glibc a JetPack board provides. Don't copy that pattern unless you also need to refuse installs on the wrong OS version.
  2. Re-solve. pixi lock solves the lock for every platform, so this is where you find out whether each dependency exists for the new one. Do it on any machine — the solve doesn't need the target OS.

  3. Add substitutes. Anything the Jetson gets from JetPack (OpenCV, TensorRT) has to come from somewhere on a laptop. Mirror what [target.osx-arm64.*] does:

    [target.linux-64.dependencies]
opencv = ">=4.13.0,<5"

[target.linux-64.pypi-dependencies]
rerun-sdk = ">=0.38.1, <0.39"

    Keep the rerun-sdk pin equal to RERUN_VERSION in utils/install_jetson_rerun.sh, so every platform speaks the same rerun wire format. 4. Install and run the smoke test:

    pixi install
pixi run python -c "import cv2, dora, rerun; print(cv2.__version__, rerun.__version__)"
pixi run dora-demo        # needs a webcam; see the camera-index note on the dora page

docs.title: Things to know
docs.text:
• Target sections don't merge with the workspace ones for activation. A [target.<p>.activation] scripts list replaces the top-level list. Right now only the Jetson has activation scripts, so there is nothing to repeat, but if a shared script is ever added at workspace level, every target that declares its own list must include it too.
  • [dependencies] is for things that resolve everywhere. If a package only exists for some platforms, it goes in a target section for each platform that has it — a package missing on any declared platform fails the whole solve.
  • No CUDA on laptops, and none declared on the Jetson either. Don't add cuda = "…" to a platform entry; the Jetson gets GPU libraries from JetPack, laptops get none (see Platforms, "Why CUDA isn't declared").
  • The lock is per-platform but one file. A change to one target section re-solves only that platform's part, but commit the whole pixi.lock — partial lock edits are how two people end up with different envs.
  • Laptops are partial support by design. GStreamer NVIDIA plugins, TensorRT, anything hardware-bound will never run there. Document the gap in Platforms instead of working around it; the Jetson (ssh juice) is where things get verified before they count as working.
  • Windows is untested. Expect the activation scripts (bash) and anything using /dev/video* to need work; WSL2 is the lower-effort route if someone needs it.

docs.title: Platforms: Jetson Orin is the main one
docs.text:
pixi.toml declares two platforms. jetson is the primary target and the one Jetson-specific work is written for; osx-arm64 (dev laptops) gets the same dora stack with substitutes where the Jetson uses hardware-specific pieces, so most things can be developed there but not all of them will run.

jetson (main) osx-arm64 (dev, partial) Hardware / OS AGX Orin, Orin NX on JetPack 7 (L4T R39.2.x): Ubuntu 24.04, glibc 2.39, CUDA 13.2 Apple Silicon Mac OpenCV JetPack's 4.8 — GStreamer 1.24 with the NVIDIA plugins (nvarguscamerasrc, nvvidconv, nvv4l2decoder, …) conda-forge 4.13 TensorRT JetPack's 10.16 (import tensorrt) — numpy 1.26 (<2, forced by JetPack's cv2) 2.x rerun-sdk pixi run install-rerun — outside the lock (see below) in the lock

jetson is a named pixi platform: it solves for the linux-aarch64 subdir but pins the virtual packages a JetPack 7 board provides (glibc = "2.39"), so pixi install on an older board (JetPack 6 = Ubuntu 22.04 / glibc 2.35) refuses instead of producing a half-working env. Jetson-only dependencies and activation live under [target.jetson.*]; laptop substitutes under [target.osx-arm64.*]. There is a single default environment, so the commands are the same on both: pixi install, pixi run …, pixi shell.

How the native OpenCV / TensorRT get in — utils/jetson_activate.sh, sourced on activation:

  1. PYTHONPATH gets /usr/lib/python3.12/dist-packages (where JetPack puts cv2 and tensorrt for the system Python) ahead of the env's site-packages, so import cv2 resolves to JetPack's build even if a conda py-opencv ever ends up in the env as a transitive dependency.
  2. LD_LIBRARY_PATH gets $CONDA_PREFIX/lib first. This is a library-mixing guard: conda's python has a transitive DT_RPATH that makes the loader pick conda copies of some of OpenCV's transitive deps, while NVIDIA's libopencv_*.so.408 (built with DT_RUNPATH) pick system copies — the two glibs then collide and import cv2 fails with libgio-2.0.so.0: undefined symbol: g_variant_builder_init_static. With the env's lib/ first, every soname both sides have consistently resolves to the (newer) conda copy; things conda doesn't have (libopencv_*.408, GTK2, ffmpeg 6, the NVIDIA stack) still come from the system.
  3. Because of (2), cv2's GStreamer is now conda's core, so GST_PLUGIN_PATH adds the system plugin dir (that's where the NVIDIA elements live) and the plugin registry is kept under the env ($CONDA_PREFIX/var/cache/gstreamer-1.0/) so it doesn't fight the system GStreamer's cache. The first scan logs one harmless warning about libgstgtk.so (wants a Wayland symbol conda's libgstgl doesn't export); it's blacklisted and never retried.

Check it on a board:

pixi run python -c "import cv2, tensorrt; print(cv2.__version__, cv2.__file__, tensorrt.__version__)"
# 4.8.0 /usr/lib/python3.12/dist-packages/cv2/__init__.py 10.16.2.10

rerun on the Jetson is installed outside the lock. JetPack's cv2 is compiled against apt numpy 1.26 and refuses to import under NumPy 2, so the Jetson target pins numpy <2; every rerun-sdk since 0.24 declares numpy>=2 (PyPI and conda-forge alike), and pixi has no way to override PyPI metadata — the two can't be in the same solve. 0.38.1 does run on numpy 1.26 (it ships a _numpy_compatibility shim; only the declared requirement blocks it), so on the Jetson:

pixi run install-rerun     # uv pip install --no-deps rerun-sdk==0.38.1 into the env; no-op once installed

utils/install_jetson_rerun.sh pins the version (keep it equal to the rerun-sdk pin in pixi.toml), and rerun's real runtime deps (attrs, pillow, psutil, typing_extensions; pyarrow comes with dora) are in the Jetson solve. The package survives pixi install re-syncs, and rerun-test depends-on the task on the Jetson so it self-heals anyway; pixi run install-rerun --force reinstalls.

Why CUDA isn't declared on the platform. Adding cuda = "13.2" to the jetson entry makes conda-forge prefer CUDA builds of anything that has them, and those bring conda's own CUDA runtime, not JetPack's (when the ROS 2 stack was in this env, slam_toolbox's ceres-solver alone flipped to a GPU build and pulled ~1 GB of conda CUDA 12.9). GPU Python packages on the Jetson should come from NVIDIA's JetPack wheels; only add cuda if a conda package genuinely needs __cuda to resolve.

Gotchas: - pixi run on the Jetson exports LD_LIBRARY_PATH=$CONDA_PREFIX/lib:…, so system binaries run through it (nvcc, tegrastats, ssh, …) also see conda's libs first. conda's are all newer than Ubuntu 24.04's, so this has been harmless, but run system tools outside pixi if one misbehaves. - To install on an aarch64 machine that isn't JetPack 7 (e.g. a container), override the check with CONDA_OVERRIDE_GLIBC=2.39 pixi install — the activation script's /usr/lib/python3.12/dist-packages and GStreamer paths won't exist there, so import cv2 will fall back to conda's py-opencv.
